value: Both are risk-management elements of the standards’ Weight and Balance task (Task C), so applicants must be able to assess them.
reason: Weight and Balance is Task C of Area I in the ACS (AM.I.C.R4, R5, p. 9), not Task B.

value: A loaded airplane weighs 2,600 lb. Its aft CG limit is +100 in, but its CG is at +100.5 in. Ballast can go at +40 in. How much is needed?
reason: “0.5 in aft of the aft limit at +100 in” can be read as the CG, not the limit, being at +100 in.

value: No legal loading can then put the loaded CG outside its range, so no adverse-loading check is needed.
reason: The old back had to be read twice (“It cannot be legally loaded so…, so…”).

value: Do machine threads seal a fitting the way tapered pipe threads do, and what makes such a connection fluid-tight?

value.alt: Fifteen fluid line identification tapes, each repeating a system name on a colour field, most with a geometric symbol column: fuel, lubrication, pneumatic, hydraulic, coolant, air condition, electrical conduit, water, compressed gas, instrument air, breathing oxygen, fire protection, de-icing, vacuum and inerting fluid. A sixteenth panel shows the skull-and-crossbones warning symbol.
value.credit: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), Figure 9-16

reason: The figure has fifteen tapes plus a warning-symbol panel, not sixteen tapes; the water tape has no symbol column.

value: Up to 2 weeks, says the handbook’s rivet section; its heat-treatment section says only “several days”.
reason: The handbook gives the refrigerated life two ways: “up to 2 weeks” (p. 7-52) and “usable for several days” (p. 7-24, pdf 268).

value: Both passages give below 32 °F; because the two figures differ, expect either in questions, and reheat-treat rivets not used in time.
reason: Explains the second figure the back now names.

value: The rivet section is stricter: 2017-T out for 1 hour or more, or 2024-T out for over 10 minutes, must be reheat-treated.
reason: The handbook gives the 2024-T limit two ways (10 to 20 minutes, p. 7-24; over 10 minutes, p. 7-54); the old explanation named neither.

value: They give more strength than a same-size 2117-T field rivet (the handbook prints “2217-T” here), but age harden at room temperature.
reason: “the field alloy” was untaught at this point; the handbook names the comparison rivet (misprinted 2217-T). Ageing: “begin to age harden within a few minutes” (p. 7-52).

value: It is one of the two icebox rivet alloys, and the one that must be driven soonest after leaving the refrigerator.
reason: The handbook does not call 2024-T the stronger icebox alloy; it gives the shorter driving time (10 to 20 minutes against about 1 hour).

value: A bin holds aluminium-alloy rivets whose heads carry a raised double dash. Which rivets are they, and how must they be handled?
reason: The figure on the front labels every marking with its alloy, giving the answer away.

value.alt: Five rivet heads seen from above, each labelled with its code and alloy: a plain head, code A, 1100; a recessed dot, code AD, 2117-T; a raised dot, code D, 2017-T; a raised double dash, code DD, 2024-T; a raised cross, code B, 5056.
value.credit: Drawn for this deck from the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), Figure 7-35 and chapter 7, Identification

reason: Moves the labelled figure to the back so it no longer gives the answer.

value: On an aircraft bolt head, what do an asterisk, a triangle and the letter “S” each identify?
reason: The figure on the front labels each head with its answer.

value.alt: Three hexagonal bolt heads seen from above. The first carries an asterisk and is labelled AN standard steel bolt. The second carries a triangle and is labelled close tolerance bolt. The third carries the letter S and is labelled special bolt.
value.credit: Drawn for this deck from the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), chapter 7, Identification and Coding and Figure 7-19

reason: Moves the labelled figure to the back so it no longer gives the answer.

value: B: an extension changes the reading needed, so the formula is mandatory. A: this multiplies by B ÷ A (12 ÷ 10) instead of A ÷ B. D: this divides the required torque by the extension length alone.
reason: 240 × 12 ÷ 10 = 288, so option A inverts the ratio (B ÷ A); the old text said “B ÷ C”, and there is no C in the formula.

value: B: the handbook gives no copper-spot test; its spot test for Inconel against stainless steel shows pink or brown. C: that separates heat-treatable from non-heat-treatable aluminium. A: titanium is nonmagnetic.
reason: The handbook’s electrochemical test uses ammonium fluoride and dimethylglyoxime and gives a pink (Inconel) or brown (stainless) spot (pp. 7-4, 7-5); no cupric chloride copper spot.

value: A part whose physical part or paperwork is questionable: a good part with bad paperwork, or a bad part with “good” (bogus) paperwork.
reason: “The middle two of four part categories” means nothing before the four are taught; the back also repeated the front’s term.
